title: Asymmetric Division: Numb and the Neuroblast

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: An asymmetric cell division produces daughters with different {{c1::fates}}.
cards.back: Different fates define asymmetry; unequal size is not required.
cards.quote: In an asymmetric division the daughters take different fates
cards.section: Two ways to make sisters differ

cards.front: How do the two kinds of symmetric division change a progenitor pool?
cards.back: Making two progenitors enlarges the pool; making two differentiating daughters spends it.
cards.quote: two progenitors, which enlarges the pool, or two cells that go on to differentiate, which spends it.
cards.section: Two ways to make sisters differ

cards.front: How do an inherited determinant and a niche create different daughter-cell fates?
cards.back: A determinant is segregated inside the mother and inherited by one daughter. A niche supplies external signals that only one daughter continues receiving.
cards.quote: The daughters start alike, but only one stays in contact with a niche
cards.section: Two ways to make sisters differ

cards.front: Two equal-sized stem-cell daughters inherit the same proteins, but only one retains contact with a stem-cell niche. What happens to their fates, and why?
cards.back: They can take different fates: the daughter in the niche remains a stem cell, while the displaced daughter differentiates because it loses the niche signal.
cards.quote: The daughter pushed out of the niche differentiates.
cards.section: Two ways to make sisters differ

cards.front: How could you distinguish unequal determinant inheritance from unequal niche contact as the cause of different daughter-cell fates?
cards.back: Compare determinant inheritance with both daughters given equivalent niche contact; separately vary niche contact while matching inheritance. Fate tracking inheritance supports an internal mechanism; fate tracking contact supports a niche mechanism. These tests use the two stated routes to asymmetry.
cards.quote: A division can become asymmetric in two ways.
cards.section: Two ways to make sisters differ

cards.front: Which four cells make up the classic simplified fly bristle lineage?
cards.back: A sensory neuron, a sheath cell, a hair cell and a socket cell.
cards.quote: A bristle is a small sense organ of four cells: a neuron, a sheath cell that wraps it, and two outer support cells

cards.front: Notch signalling requires {{c1::cell contact}} because its ligand is on a neighbouring cell’s surface.
cards.back: Delta is one such surface ligand.
cards.quote: Notch is a receptor that signals only between touching cells
cards.section: Notch splits the lineage at every division

cards.front: How does activation of the surface receptor Notch lead to changes in gene expression?
cards.back: Activated Notch is cut, allowing its inner part to switch genes on.
cards.quote: When Notch is activated it is cut, so that its inner part can switch genes on.
cards.section: Notch splits the lineage at every division

cards.front: Early Notch inactivation in fly pupae yields extra bristle precursors that form normal bristles; later inactivation yields neuron-only organs. What distinct roles do these results reveal?
cards.back: Notch first restricts which cells become sensory organ precursors, then selects different fates among their descendants. The different outcomes depend on when Notch is removed.
cards.quote: Notch is used once to pick the precursor, and again to split its progeny.
cards.section: Notch splits the lineage at every division

cards.front: In the classic four-cell fly bristle scheme, Notch is absent throughout the sensory organ precursor lineage. What cells result, and why?
cards.back: Four neurons and no hair, socket or sheath result. The precursor makes two inner precursors, and each makes two neurons because every choice is Notch-off.
cards.quote: With no Notch, the SOP gives two inner precursors instead of one of each. Each inner precursor then gives two neurons
cards.section: Notch splits the lineage at every division

cards.front: At the first division of a fly sensory organ precursor, which branch is Notch-on?
cards.back: The outer precursor (pIIa), which produces the hair and socket cells.
cards.quote: the outer branch, which makes the shaft and socket, needs Notch.
cards.section: Notch splits the lineage at every division

cards.front: In the classic fly bristle lineage, the outer precursor’s Notch-on daughter becomes the {{c1::socket cell}}.
cards.back: The hair cell is its Notch-off sister.
cards.quote: Numb goes into the Notch-off daughter, the inner precursor at the first division, then the hair cell, then the neuron.

cards.front: In the classic fly bristle lineage, the inner branch’s Notch-on daughter becomes the {{c1::sheath cell}}.
cards.back: The neuron is its Notch-off sister.
cards.quote: Each inner precursor then gives two neurons instead of a neuron and a sheath cell.
cards.section: Notch splits the lineage at every division

cards.front: What did antibody staining of dividing fly sensory organ precursors show about Numb inheritance?
cards.back: Numb formed a membrane-associated crescent on one side and passed into only one daughter, the inner precursor in the classic scheme.
cards.quote: lay in a crescent on one half of the cell, and when the cell divided it went into one daughter only.

cards.front: Numb is absent from a fly sensory organ precursor and all its descendants, while Notch signalling remains available. What happens to the classic bristle lineage, and why?
cards.back: It produces four outer support cells and no neuron or sheath. Without the Numb veto, both daughters take the Notch-on choice at each division.
cards.quote: Without Numb, the lineage made four outer support cells and no neuron or sheath.

cards.front: In the classic simplified fly bristle scheme, both daughters inherit Numb at only the first division of a sensory organ precursor; later divisions sort Numb normally. What cells form, and why?
cards.back: Two neurons and two sheath cells form, with no hair or socket. Both first daughters become inner precursors, but each later produces its normal neuron–sheath pair.
cards.quote: both daughters became inner precursors, and each divided as an inner precursor does, giving neurons and sheath cells but no hair or socket

cards.front: Why is Numb described as a veto on Notch in fly sister-cell fate choices?
cards.back: It blocks Notch rather than specifying a particular cell type. Its recipient takes the Notch-off fate available at that division.
cards.quote: It only blocks Notch, so a cell with Numb takes whatever fate a cell without Notch would take.

cards.front: Comparing a double mutant’s phenotype with those of the single mutants is called {{c1::epistasis analysis}}.
cards.back: The comparison can help distinguish models of how the genes act.
cards.quote: (This reading of a double mutant is called epistasis analysis.)

cards.front: Fly MP2 precursors lacking both Notch and Numb make two dMP2 neurons. The Notch single mutant does too. What does this establish about Numb’s proposed instruction to become dMP2?
cards.back: Numb is not a required dMP2 instruction: dMP2 cells form without it. Matching the Notch mutant supports Numb acting as a veto on Notch in this choice.
cards.quote: Numb is not needed to make dMP2. It is needed only to stop Notch.

cards.front: A daughter-cell protein affects fate solely by inhibiting a signalling receptor. If the receptor is already absent, what happens when the inhibitor is also removed, and why?
cards.back: Removing the inhibitor makes no additional difference to that fate choice. With no receptor signal left to inhibit, its veto has no target.
cards.quote: with no Notch, Numb changes nothing.

cards.front: A hypothetical fate regulator lacking one domain still forms a normal cortical crescent but no longer blocks receptor signalling. What can you infer about localization and function?
cards.back: Crescent formation and signal inhibition are separable functions; localization alone does not establish activity. The deleted domain is required for inhibition in this assay. This applies the rule that reaching one side and vetoing a signal are separate jobs.
cards.quote: so getting to one side and vetoing Notch are separate jobs.

cards.front: Why does Notch-on not always mean stem-cell self-renewal in fly neural lineages?
cards.back: In the bristle and MP2 lineages both sisters differentiate. Notch selects between sister fates; it maintains progenitor character only in some contexts.
cards.quote: In these lineages both sisters go on to differentiate

cards.front: What are the two daughters of a typical type I fly neuroblast division?
cards.back: A large apical neuroblast and a small basal ganglion mother cell (GMC); the GMC divides once more into two neurons or glia.
cards.quote: a large apical daughter stays a neuroblast, and a small basal daughter, the ganglion mother cell (GMC), divides once more
cards.section: How the neuroblast picks a side

cards.front: Prospero’s cortical localization in dividing fly neuroblasts persists without microtubules. What does that imply about the proposal that the spindle carries Prospero into position?
cards.back: Spindle transport is not required for that localization. A separate cortical positioning system is implicated, even though the crescent’s location tracks one centrosome.
cards.quote: Its localization followed the position of one centrosome but did not need microtubules, so it was not carried into place along the spindle.
cards.section: How the neuroblast picks a side

cards.front: Which proteins form the apical Par complex in a fly neuroblast?
cards.back: Bazooka (fly Par3), Par6 and aPKC.
cards.quote: with Pins and the Par complex together at the apical side and Numb opposite.

cards.front: How do Inscuteable, Pins, Gαi and Mud connect the apical cortex to spindle orientation in a fly neuroblast?
cards.back: Inscuteable joins the apical complex and recruits Pins. Pins, Gαi and Mud anchor dynein apically, where it pulls on microtubules from one spindle pole.
cards.quote: Step 2 lines the spindle up along the apical-basal axis, so the furrow cuts between top and bottom and the basal cargo goes to one daughter.
cards.section: How the neuroblast picks a side

cards.front: How does apical aPKC activity keep Numb and Miranda at the basal cortex of a dividing fly neuroblast?
cards.back: aPKC phosphorylates Lgl, Numb and Miranda apically, causing cortical release there. Because aPKC acts at the top, Numb and Miranda remain bound basally.
cards.quote: aPKC phosphorylates Lgl and releases it from the apical membrane.
cards.section: How the neuroblast picks a side

cards.front: Which adaptors localize Prospero, Brat and Numb to the basal cortex of a fly neuroblast?
cards.back: Miranda carries Prospero and Brat; Partner of Numb (Pon) localizes Numb.
cards.quote: Without Miranda, Prospero and Brat lose their crescent at the basal cortex
cards.section: How the neuroblast picks a side

cards.front: How does inherited Prospero help a fly ganglion mother cell stop self-renewing?
cards.back: After division, Prospero enters the GMC nucleus and shuts down genes for self-renewal and division.
cards.quote: After the division, Prospero enters the GMC's nucleus and shuts down genes for self-renewal and division.
cards.section: How the neuroblast picks a side

cards.front: A fly neuroblast lacks Miranda but retains spindle-orienting machinery. What happens to Prospero and Brat localization, and must the spindle also be misoriented?
cards.back: Their basal crescent is lost; their eventual positions depend on stage and lineage. The spindle need not change because Miranda carries cargo rather than aiming the spindle.
cards.quote: Losing Miranda need not change the spindle, because Miranda carries cargo and is not part of the system that aims the spindle.
cards.section: How the neuroblast picks a side

cards.front: A hypothetical stem cell has a correctly aligned spindle, but its small daughter fails to receive proteins that limit self-renewal and keeps dividing. Does spindle alignment alone demonstrate normal asymmetric fate control?
cards.back: No. Correct orientation and successful cargo delivery are separate requirements. Check where the proteins localize and which daughter inherits them. The inference combines the spindle-orientation rule with the rule that missing differentiation cargo can allow continued self-renewal.
cards.quote: If the small daughter does not get them, it can fail to stop self-renewing and keep dividing like a neuroblast.
cards.section: How the neuroblast picks a side

cards.front: What did transplantation of larval brain tissue from pins, miranda, numb or prospero mutant flies demonstrate about faulty division machinery?
cards.back: The mutant tissue could produce invasive, lethal overgrowth exceeding a hundred times its starting size, showing a possible long-term consequence of disrupted fate control.
cards.quote: It grew to more than a hundred times its starting size, into invasive, lethal overgrowth.

cards.front: How do the main tumour origins differ between fly brat and prospero mutants?
cards.back: brat tumours arise mainly from type II intermediate progenitors that fail to mature; prospero tumours arise from ganglion mother cells.
cards.quote: brat tumours arise mainly in type II lineages, from intermediate progenitors that fail to mature, whereas prospero tumours arise from GMCs.

cards.front: Why does a small, repeated failure of daughter-cell differentiation cause compounding growth in the simple stem-cell model?
cards.back: Each retained stem-cell daughter joins the dividing pool. Every stem cell divides each round, so the expected pool is multiplied by 1 + f (f is the probability that a small daughter stays a stem cell), not increased by a fixed amount.
cards.quote: With a leak, every round multiplies the average number of neuroblasts by (1 + f), so the count compounds.

cards.front: In the simple type I neuroblast model, one neuroblast completes 50 rounds with perfect sorting. How many neuroblasts remain, and how many neurons or glia are produced if every GMC divides and all progeny survive?
cards.back: Neuroblasts: 1 × (1 + 0)^50 = 1. GMCs produced: 1 × 50 = 50. Each gives two differentiated cells, so output = 50 × 2 = 100 neurons or glia.
cards.quote: over 50 rounds it makes 50 GMCs, which divide into 100 neurons or glia if all survive.

cards.front: In the illustrative neuroblast model, start with one neuroblast. Each small daughter has probability f = 0.10 of remaining a neuroblast; all neuroblasts divide every round and none die or stop. What is the expected neuroblast count after 50 rounds?
cards.back: Expected count = N₀(1 + f)^n = 1 × 1.10^50 ≈ 117 neuroblasts. This is an average across lineages, not a guaranteed integer count for any one lineage.
cards.quote: A leak of one in ten gives, on average, more than a hundred neuroblasts after 50 rounds.

cards.front: The leaky-sorting model yields more than a hundred neuroblasts, and mutant fly brain transplants grew more than a hundredfold. Does the numerical similarity establish a quantitative fit?
cards.back: No. The stated model counts neuroblasts, whereas the experiment measured tissue growth. Its rounds are illustrative, and the transplants grew in adult hosts. The compounding rule explains how growth can amplify; it does not calibrate the experiment.
cards.quote: The model counts neuroblasts, not tissue size

cards.front: One mouse Numb/Numblike deletion study exhausted cortical progenitors, while another produced overproliferation; deletion region and timing differed. What follow-up design would help interpret this conflict?
cards.back: Vary deletion timing while holding region fixed, and region while holding timing fixed. Assess Notch activity alongside progenitor behaviour. This combines the stated timing/region differences with Numb’s additional junction and endocytosis roles; the existing phenotypes alone do not establish a Notch-veto mechanism.
cards.quote: a mouse phenotype is not automatically a Notch veto.

cards.front: A tissue’s stem cells depend on a niche. If the niche itself is destroyed, what happens to its stem-cell population, and why?
cards.back: The resident stem cells tend to differentiate and are not replaced, because the local support needed to maintain the stem-cell population is gone.
cards.quote: if the niche itself is lost, the stem cells it held are not replaced.

cards.front: In a hypothetical tissue, daughter fates depend entirely on niche contact. A division leaves both daughters in the niche rather than displacing one. What happens to stem-cell maintenance versus differentiation, and why?
cards.back: Both daughters can remain stem cells, expanding the pool while reducing that division’s differentiating output. This combines the niche rule—contact maintains stem-cell character—with the rule that making two progenitors enlarges the pool.
cards.quote: The daughters start alike, but only one stays in contact with a niche
cards.section: Two ways to make sisters differ

cards.front: How do the division axis and Pins–Par relationship differ between a fly sensory organ precursor and a neuroblast?
cards.back: The precursor divides head-to-tail within the epithelium, with Pins opposite Par. The neuroblast divides apical-to-basal, perpendicular to the epithelium, with Pins and Par together apically.
cards.quote: Pins sits opposite the Par proteins in one cell and with them in the other.

cards.front: In the fly sense-organ endocytosis model, Numb still enters one daughter, but its ability to prevent Notch and Sanpodo recycling is selectively lost. What happens to surface Notch, and why?
cards.back: Surface Notch should be higher than with an intact veto because internalized Notch and Sanpodo can return to the surface. With ligand available, the daughter may regain Notch signalling.
cards.quote: they are kept from recycling back to it, which lowers Notch at that cell's surface.

cards.front: Which fly neuroblast lineages most clearly depend on active Notch to retain progenitor character?
cards.back: Larval type II lineages; Notch loss has milder effects in type I neuroblasts, and embryonic neuroblasts do not share the same dependence.
cards.quote: the daughter that keeps Notch active keeps progenitor character most clearly in type II lineages.

cards.front: How does the revised adult fly bristle lineage change the classic neuron–sheath branch?
cards.back: pIIb first produces a glial cell and pIIIb; pIIIb then makes the neuron and sheath. The adult lineage therefore has five cells and four divisions.
cards.quote: the inner precursor (pIIb) first divides into a glial cell and a cell called pIIIb, which divides again to make the neuron and sheath.
